<reason>Both sides argued well, but PRO built the cleaner route to victory on the motion as written. PRO's decisive frame — that the motion only claims consent is necessary, not sufficient, and that every protection CON proposed (union floors, retention caps, no-resale, "ask in the agreement") is itself disclosed, specific and negotiated, i.e. the opposite of broad boilerplate — was never squarely answered. CON never defended the "all media now known or hereafter devised" clause the motion actually targets, and its counter-model conceded that broad boilerplate is inadequate. PRO also converted CON's own pressure question into its best weighing: a non-waivable floor with no consent requirement still permits studios to synthesize every performer's voice into forty languages without ever asking, which is precisely the silent taking at issue. CON's two strongest strikes were real: the dilemma that a collectively bargained AI-approval requirement is itself a contract term (so the motion "forbids nothing"), and the non-response problem for catalogue titles. PRO's answers (specific, bounded, per-use affirmative approval is exactly the distinction the motion draws; silence should not default to yes; non-response is a logistics problem) were adequate rather than airtight, but sufficient. CON also underdeveloped its strongest substantive anchor — that dubbing merely carries an already-licensed performance — after PRO's sharp reply that traditional dubbing hired a second, separately paid actor and never extracted vocal identity. CON's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a further execution cost, and its "opt-in is ceremony" closing, while memorable, relied on a concession PRO had already bounded.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's answer to CON's pressure questions (A4.3–A4.4): accepting non-waivable retention and no-resale limits while showing they concede nothing, because a floor alone still lets a studio synthesize every performer's voice into forty languages without ever asking. This turned CON's "substance not permission" framing into evidence that CON's model cannot prevent the core harm, while PRO's "boilerplate never defended" point kept the motion's actual comparison alive.</best_rebuttal>
